title: The soul of the world
hookLine: an old letter to a man called Diognetus says Christians live in their own countries as sojourners, and are to the world what the soul is to the body
carry: every homeland foreign, every foreign land home

lines: NO SPECIAL CITY, NO SPECIAL LANGUAGE.
cards: A man named Diognetus has questions. Who are these Christians? What God do they trust?
Why don't they fear death, and why do they love each other like that? Somebody writes him an answer, and doesn't sign it. We learn little about Diognetus, either.
The letter describes the Christians around it the way you'd describe neighbors to a visitor. They don't live in their own cities or speak a special language.
They eat the ordinary food and wear the ordinary clothes of wherever they live. You couldn't pick them out in a crowd. Then the letter says something strange about where they belong.

teach.b: In paraphrase: Christians live in their own countries, but as sojourners. They take part in everything as citizens and put up with everything as foreigners.
Every foreign land is a homeland to them, and every homeland a foreign land. They marry and have children like everyone else. They obey the laws, and in their own lives go beyond them.
Mistreated, they bless. The idea is older than the letter.
The first letter of Peter, in the King James Bible, writes to believers "as strangers and pilgrims." Hebrews says the faithful of old "confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth."
The letter turns that idea into a way of living in a city.

teach.h: WHAT THE SOUL IS TO THE BODY.
teach.b: Then its boldest picture: what the soul is to the body, Christians are to the world. The soul is spread through every part of the body, and Christians through every city. The soul lives in the body but isn't of it.
The body even resents the soul, and still the soul holds it together. Some readers find that claim too big for any group to live up to.
Others hear it as a job description, not a boast: be in the city, care for the city, and don't let it be the whole of you.

teach.h: SEEK THE PEACE OF THE CITY.
teach.b: The prophet Jeremiah had told exiles in Babylon, "seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives." Stranger and citizen at once.

how: Some Christians draw on the letter to Diognetus and on 1 Peter's 'strangers and pilgrims' when they talk about belonging to a city while also belonging to God, and some churches pray for their towns and local leaders in their services.

games.q: you're a Christian in the city the letter describes. your neighbors don't share your faith. how does the letter say you live?
o: move away and build a town of your own.
live as a citizen and a sojourner at once.
blend in until nothing about you is different.
games.why: they share in everything as citizens and put up with everything as foreigners. every homeland foreign, every foreign land home.

practice: Picture the place you live, your street, your building, your town, and name one small, ordinary thing you could do for it, like checking on a neighbor.
Then notice one way the place pulls at you that you'd rather not follow, and hold both. If you pray, name your town to God, street by street; if you don't, simply wish it well.

wordCard.voice: Diognetus. The man whose questions prompted a letter saying what the soul is to the body, Christians are to the world: spread through it, holding it together, never quite at home.

orig.note: Greek: one living beside, a resident foreigner. 1 Peter 2:11 calls believers this, the word behind 'strangers'.

carryVoice: Your line: every homeland foreign, every foreign land home. In the city, and never only of it. See you tomorrow.
